opts: Everything beyond the Earth's air, where there is almost nothing to breathe
quiz.why: Space is what lies beyond the atmosphere. It is almost empty, with no air to breathe. Picking 'the air above the clouds' is a common mix-up, but the air goes on far above the clouds before it thins out.

quiz.p: Shreya covers a candle with a jar and it goes out. Why?
opts: The flame runs short of oxygen
The jar is made of glass
quiz.why: A flame needs oxygen. Under the jar, no fresh air gets in, so the flame goes out when the oxygen near it runs low.

quiz.p: Why does a rocket carry its own oxygen?
opts: Because in space there is no air, and its fuel cannot burn without oxygen
quiz.why: Like the candle under the jar, the rocket's fire needs oxygen. Above the air there is none to take in, so the rocket brings it.

quiz.p: A rocket lifts off. What pushes it up?
opts: The hot gas it pushes down out of its engine, which pushes back on it
quiz.why: The rocket pushes the gas down and the gas pushes the rocket up. This works in space too, where there is no air.

quiz.p: Why is a rocket built in stages?
opts: So that empty tanks can be dropped and the rocket gets lighter
So it can be painted in parts
quiz.why: When a stage's fuel is used up, it is dropped. The rest of the rocket is lighter, so its fuel can push it faster.

quiz.p: Why do the biggest telescopes have huge mirrors?
opts: To collect lots of light, so faint stars and galaxies show up
To make stars look like big balls
So they can see in the daytime
quiz.why: A bigger mirror catches more light. Stars stay as points in any telescope. What a big mirror gives is a brighter picture of faint things.

quiz.p: You cover half of a magnifying glass that is making a picture of a window. What happens to the picture?
opts: It stays whole but gets dimmer
It turns the right way up
quiz.why: Every part of the lens gathers light from the whole window. Covering half lets in half the light, so the picture dims but stays whole.

quiz.p: Which of these do astronauts on the space station clean and use again?
quiz.why: Most of the station's water is cleaned and used again, even the water from sweat and urine. Food is eaten, so new food must come from Earth.

quiz.p: Why does a spacesuit have a pack on its back?
opts: To hold the astronaut's own air and keep them at a safe temperature
quiz.why: Outside the spacecraft there is no air. The pack gives the astronaut oxygen and keeps the suit at a safe temperature.

opts: It landed near the Moon's south pole and drove a rover there
quiz.why: Chandrayaan-3's lander Vikram landed near the south pole on 23 August 2023, and its rover Pragyan drove about 100 metres. Mangalyaan was the Mars mission.

quiz.p: Who was the first Indian to travel into space?
quiz.why: Rakesh Sharma flew in 1984. Kalpana Chawla flew later, in 1997, as an American astronaut. Vikram Sarabhai started India's space programme but did not go to space.

quiz.p: Before 2009, most scientists thought the Moon had no water at all. What did India's Chandrayaan-1 help show?
opts: There are thin traces of water in the Moon's dust, and later its data showed ice in dark polar craters
The Moon is made of ice
quiz.why: An instrument on Chandrayaan-1 found the gap in reflected light that water leaves. The traces are thin, and the ice is in craters that never see sunlight.

items.p: Where does space begin, by the line many scientists use?
opts: At the top of the clouds, about 2 km up
items.why: Many scientists use 100 km as the edge of space. Clouds are much lower, and the Moon is about 384,000 km away. A strong answer knows the air thins out slowly, so 100 km is an agreed line, not a wall.

items.p: A rocket must carry its own ____, because there is no air in space and fuel cannot burn without it.
items.why: Burning is fuel joining with oxygen. In space there is no air to give oxygen, so the rocket brings it.

items.p: Revathi, a girl in Class 3, covers a tealight with a small glass. The flame goes out after 8 seconds. She tries again with a big jar. What will most likely happen?
opts: The flame goes out at once
The flame lasts longer than 8 seconds
The flame lasts exactly 8 seconds again
items.why: A big jar holds more air, so the flame has more oxygen to use before it runs low. A strong answer says why: more air, more oxygen.

items.p: In the jar test, the flame went out even though there was still wax left in the candle. Explain why.
items.a: The flame needs oxygen as well as wax. Under the jar, no fresh air could get in. The flame used up the oxygen near the wick, and when too little was left, it went out. The wax was still there, but it could not burn without oxygen.
items.why: A strong answer names both things a flame needs, fuel and oxygen, and says which one ran out.

items.p: Astronauts on the space station float because there is no gravity up there.
items.why: False. Gravity at the station's height is about nine tenths as strong as on the ground. The station and everyone in it are falling round the Earth together, so they float inside it.

items.p: Match each Indian mission to what it did.
pairs: went round the Moon and helped find water there
reached Mars on India's first try
landed near the Moon's south pole
watches the Sun from far out in space
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These five missions show India's path from a first satellite to the Moon, Mars and the Sun.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one need air from around it to work, or can it work in space?
items: a plane
Needs air around it
a rocket
Can work in space
a candle with no jar
Needs air around it
a kite
Needs air around it
a telescope
Can work in space
a satellite
Can work in space
a ceiling fan's breeze
Needs air around it
an astronaut in a spacesuit
Can work in space
items.a: see items
items.why: Planes, kites and fans push on the air, and a candle burns its oxygen. A rocket carries its own oxygen, and a spacesuit carries its own air. A strong sorter asks: does it take something from the air around it?

items.p: What is a telescope's main job?
opts: To make stars look like big balls
To collect more light than our eyes can
items.why: A big lens or mirror catches much more light than the small pupil of the eye, so faint things show up. Stars stay as points even in huge telescopes.

items.p: Gayathri, a girl in Class 3, covers half of a magnifying glass while it makes a picture of a window. She thinks half the window will vanish from the picture. What really happens, and why?
items.a: The whole window stays in the picture, but it gets dimmer. Light from every part of the window goes through every part of the lens. So the half that is still open can make the whole picture, with less light.
items.why: A strong answer says the picture stays whole and only dims, and gives the reason: every part of the lens gets light from the whole window.

items.p: Draw a rocket going up. Draw an arrow to show which way the hot gas goes, and another arrow to show which way the rocket goes.
items.a: A rocket with a big arrow pointing down out of its engine for the gas, and a big arrow pointing up on the rocket.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the two arrows pointing opposite ways. The rocket pushes the gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up.
items.art: A blank box with a small launch pad drawn at the bottom.

items.p: Chandrayaan-3's lander was called Vikram, and its rover was called ____.
items.why: Pragyan drove about 100 metres on the Moon in 2023 and tested the soil.

items.p: A plane could fly to the Moon if it carried enough fuel.
items.why: False. A plane's wings need air to push on, and its engines take oxygen from the air. Above about 100 km there is almost no air, so neither would work.

items.p: Which of these must astronauts on the space station bring up from Earth?
items.why: Food cannot be made on the station in the amounts needed, so it comes from Earth in packets. Sunlight reaches the station on its own, and gravity is there too.

items.p: On a lime-sized Earth, space begins about four sheets of paper above the skin. What does this tell you about the air we breathe?
items.a: The air is a very thin layer, close to the ground. Almost all of the air is near the Earth, and only a short way up it thins out to nothing.
items.why: A strong answer says the air is thin compared with the size of the Earth, and that space is close above us.

items.p: Label the picture of a rocket: fuel tank, oxygen tank, engine, hot gas, satellite.
items.a: The satellite is at the top. Below it are the fuel tank and the oxygen tank. The engine is at the bottom, and the hot gas comes out below the engine.
items.why: A strong labeller puts the two tanks above the engine, because the engine burns fuel with the oxygen, and the satellite at the top.
items.art: A cut-away rocket with five blank label lines pointing to the nose, two tanks, the engine and the flame below.

items.p: Why do you think India chose to land Chandrayaan-3 near the Moon's south pole, and not in a sunny spot near the middle?
items.a: Near the south pole there are deep craters that never get sunlight. Ice can last there, so it is a good place to look for water. Water could one day give astronauts drinking water and oxygen.
items.why: A strong answer links the dark craters, the cold, and the ice, and says why water matters.

items.p: Nila, a girl in Class 4, times a candle under three jars. A small glass holds 1 tumbler of water, a big glass holds 2, and a pickle jar holds 5. Under the small glass the flame lasts 8 seconds. About how long will it last under the pickle jar?
items.why: The pickle jar holds about 5 times as much air, so the flame lasts about 5 times as long, about 40 seconds. Real results wobble a little. 400 seconds would need 50 times the air.

items.p: Hamsa, a boy in Class 3, did the jar test only once with each jar. His big jar gave a shorter time than his small glass. What might have gone wrong, and what should he do?
items.a: He might not have let fresh air back into the big jar, or he started the timer late, or the flame was still small when he covered it. He should do three tries with each jar, wave each jar in the air between tries, and start timing the moment the rim touches the plate.
items.why: A strong answer names a likely mistake and says that repeating tries and keeping things the same makes the test fair.

items.p: India is deciding how to explore the Moon next.

views.says: Send more robot rovers. They need no air or food, and no one gets hurt if a landing fails.
Send people. A person notices odd things at once and can fix a problem on the spot.
The money would help more people if it were spent on schools here.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing that another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and backs it with a fact, such as: Pragyan worked on the Moon with no air, or a person can react at once, while a message to a Mars rover takes minutes. It then admits a fair point from another side, such as the cost.
items.why: This is a real argument with real trade-offs: safety and cost against the skill of people, and space spending against other needs.

items.p: Why do stars twinkle when we look at them from the ground?
opts: Moving air bends their light this way and that
items.why: The air above us is always moving, and it bends starlight a little differently from moment to moment. A telescope in space, above the air, sees stars as steady points.

items.p: A rocket in space can speed up even though there is no air to push against.
items.why: True. A rocket pushes its own hot gas out of the back, and the gas pushes the rocket forward. It does not need air for this.

items.p: Put these in order, from closest to the ground to furthest away.
items: the Moon
a plane
the space station
the edge of space
items.why: Planes fly about 11 km up. Space begins about 100 km up. The space station is about 400 km up. The Moon is about 384,000 km away.

items.p: Karthik, a boy in Class 3, says, "A rocket needs a huge jar of air from the launch pad, so that its fuel can burn." What would you tell him?
items.a: Ordinary air is only about one fifth oxygen, and a gas takes up a lot of room. A rocket carries pure oxygen instead, often as a very cold liquid, so a lot of oxygen fits in a small tank. Some rockets use a solid fuel with an oxygen-giving chemical mixed in.
items.why: A strong answer agrees that the rocket needs oxygen, but explains why carrying plain air would be far too bulky.

items.p: Draw what you saw in the half-lens test, two times: with the whole lens open, and with half of it covered. Shade them to show the brightness.
items.a: Two pictures of the whole window, upside down. The second is shaded darker but is complete.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the whole window both times, with only the brightness changed.
items.art: Two empty rectangles side by side, labelled 'whole lens' and 'half covered'.

items.p: On the space station, oxygen is made by splitting water. Where did that water come from?
opts: From Earth, carried up on rockets, and then cleaned and used again
items.why: There is no water floating in space near the station. It came from Earth, and most of it is cleaned and used again and again, even the water from sweat and urine.

items.p: A path that goes round and round a planet, like the space station's path round the Earth, is called an ____.
items.why: The space station's orbit takes it round the Earth about every 90 minutes.

items.p: In the ice test, Pooja put one ice cube in sunlight and one in the shadow of a book. Which one is most like ice in a dark crater on the Moon?
items.why: The shaded cube gets no direct sunlight, like the floor of a deep polar crater. It melted more slowly. On the Moon, with almost no air to carry warmth in, the crater ice can last for a very long time.

items.p: A message to a rover on Mars can take about 20 minutes to arrive. Explain why a team on Earth cannot steer it like a toy car.
items.a: If the rover is heading for a rock, the team will see it only about 20 minutes late, and their order to stop will take another 20 minutes to arrive. By then it is too late. So teams plan the drive ahead and let the rover check for dangers itself.
items.why: A strong answer counts the delay both ways: the picture coming back, and the order going out.

items.p: Kalpana Chawla, an astronaut who flew on American space shuttles, was born in India.
items.why: True. She was born in Karnal, in Haryana, and later became an American citizen. She flew in 1997 and in 2003.

items.p: Why does a rocket drop its first stage after a few minutes?
opts: It has burned all its fuel, and carrying the empty tank would waste the rest
To leave a gift in the sea
items.why: An empty stage is heavy and useless. Dropping it lets the next engine push a lighter rocket faster.

items.p: In the jar test, the flame went out long before all the air in the jar was gone. Air is mostly not oxygen anyway. So why does a bigger jar still help?
items.a: A flame stops when the oxygen near it gets too low, not when it is all gone. A bigger jar has more oxygen to start with, so it takes longer for the oxygen to drop that low. The other gases in the air, mostly nitrogen, do not help the flame.
items.why: A strong answer understands that the flame needs enough oxygen near it, and that a bigger jar holds more of it.

items.p: Sruthi does the jar test with two tealights side by side under the same big jar. What do you predict?
opts: They go out sooner than one tealight would
items.why: Two flames use oxygen twice as fast. The same jar has the same amount of oxygen, so it runs low sooner. A strong answer links the speed of using oxygen with the amount there is.

items.p: A family is talking about why astronauts float on the space station.

views.says: There is no gravity up there, so nothing pulls them down.
There is gravity, but they are falling all the time, together with the station.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a fact that supports your side. Then say why the other idea is easy to believe.
items.a: Kavya is right. Gravity at the station's height is about nine tenths of what it is on the ground. The station moves sideways so fast that as it falls, the Earth curves away below it, so it keeps falling round and round. Appa's idea is easy to believe because astronauts look as if nothing is pulling them.
items.why: This is a very common idea that turns out to be wrong. A strong answer gives the evidence and is fair to why people believe the other view.

items.p: Aditi points two telescopes at the same faint galaxy. One has a mirror 1 metre across, the other 2 metres across. What will the 2 metre telescope show?
opts: The same, because both are telescopes
A brighter picture, because the bigger mirror collects more light
items.why: A mirror twice as wide has about four times the area, so it collects about four times as much light. Faint things look brighter and clearer.

items.p: Covering half of a lens made the picture dimmer but did not cut it in half. Use this to explain why it does not matter much if a big telescope mirror is made of several pieces fitted together.
items.a: Every part of a lens or mirror gathers light from the whole view. So each piece of a mirror helps make the whole picture. Fitting pieces together makes one big collecting surface. The James Webb Space Telescope's mirror is made of 18 pieces.
items.why: A strong answer uses the half-lens result: each part makes the whole picture, so pieces add up their light.

items.p: Put these steps of a rocket launch in order.
items: the satellite separates and goes into orbit
the engines light and the rocket lifts off
the first stage burns out and drops away
the countdown reaches zero
a: the engines light and the rocket lifts off
the first stage burns out and drops away
the satellite separates and goes into orbit
items.why: A launch goes from countdown, to lift-off, to dropping empty stages, to letting the satellite go once it is high and fast enough.

items.p: On the Moon, a candle could burn if you lit it outside the lander.
items.why: False. The Moon has almost no air, so there is no oxygen for the flame. A candle would not stay lit, just as the flame under the jar went out when its oxygen ran low.

items.p: Draw a Moon home with an airlock. Show the two doors and where the astronaut stands between them.
items.a: A sealed home with a small room on one side. The small room has an inner door into the home and an outer door to the Moon. The astronaut stands in the small room with both doors shut.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that only one door is open at a time, so the home's air never rushes out.
items.art: A blank box with a grey Moon ground line at the bottom.

items.p: Why are the best ground telescopes often built on high mountains, like the one at Hanle in Ladakh?
opts: To be closer to the stars
There is less air above them to blur the light, and fewer clouds
items.why: A mountain top has less air above it, so less blurring and twinkling, and it is often above the clouds. Being a few kilometres closer to stars that are trillions of kilometres away makes no difference.

items.p: Some people say spending money on space is a waste. Give one way that satellites help people in India on the ground, and say whether you think that makes the spending worth it.
items.a: Weather satellites track cyclones, so people on the coast can be moved to safety in time. Satellites also help fishing boats find fish, help with maps on phones, and carry TV signals. A strong answer then gives an honest opinion with a reason.
items.why: This question asks for a fact and an opinion. A strong answer keeps them apart and gives a reason for the opinion.

items.p: India's spacecraft that watches the Sun from about 1.5 million km away is called ____.
items.why: Aditya means the Sun. It was launched in 2023 and watches the Sun all the time, with no night and no clouds in the way.

items.p: Before 2009, most scientists thought the Moon was completely dry. What helped change their minds?
opts: Chandrayaan-1's instrument found the gap in reflected light that water leaves
People saw clouds on the Moon
items.why: The Moon Mineralogy Mapper on Chandrayaan-1 measured sunlight bouncing off the Moon. Water soaks up some kinds of light, which leaves a gap. That gap showed up over large parts of the Moon.

items.p: An astronaut breathes in a little less than 1 kg of oxygen a day. Why would a crew of 4 on a 6-month trip to Mars have a much harder job than a crew on the space station?
items.a: On the space station, new supplies can come up from Earth every few months. On a long trip to Mars, nothing new can be sent, so all the oxygen, water and food must be carried or made and recycled on board for the whole journey. For 4 people that is close to 4 kg of oxygen a day, which over 6 months is more than 700 kg.
items.why: A strong answer notices that a far trip cannot be refilled, and uses the numbers to show how much would be needed.

items.p: Label the picture of a spacesuit: helmet, oxygen pack, gloves, visor.
items.a: The helmet is round the head, with the visor at the front. The oxygen pack is on the back. The gloves are on the hands.
items.why: A strong labeller puts the oxygen pack on the back, because the suit carries its own air.
items.art: An astronaut in a white spacesuit with four blank label lines.

items.p: A rocket's roar can be heard by a spacecraft floating nearby in space.
items.why: False. Sound travels by shaking the air. In space there is almost no air, so the sound cannot cross the gap.

applications: Weather satellites track cyclones over the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea, so people can be moved to safety.
Satellites carry TV signals to dish antennas on rooftops across India.
Phone maps find where you are using signals from navigation satellites. India has its own system, called NavIC.
Fishing boats in Kerala and Tamil Nadu get advice on where fish are likely to be, made using satellite pictures of the sea.
Satellite pictures help farmers and the government watch crops, floods and forest fires.
Hospitals use oxygen cylinders, like the oxygen tanks that rockets and astronauts carry.
Ideas made for space, such as water cleaners and light, strong materials, are used on Earth too.
Telescopes on Earth and in space find asteroids that come close to the Earth, so we know where they are going.

open_questions.q: How much water is there on the Moon, and could people use it?
open_questions.why_open: We know there is ice in dark polar craters, but not how much or how easy it would be to dig out.

open_questions.q: Can people stay healthy on a trip to Mars and back?
open_questions.why_open: A trip would take more than a year and a half. Nobody yet knows how to keep bones, muscles and eyes healthy, and protect against radiation, for that long.

open_questions.q: Is there life anywhere else, and could a telescope find it?
open_questions.why_open: New telescopes can study the air of planets around other stars. Nobody knows yet whether any of them have signs of life.

open_questions.q: Could people make oxygen from Moon rock?
open_questions.why_open: Moon rock is nearly half oxygen by weight, locked in minerals. Small tests work in laboratories, but nobody has yet done it on the Moon.

maths.problem: In the jar test, Deepa's small glass held 1 tumbler of water and kept the flame alight for 7 seconds. Her pickle jar held 4 tumblers. If the time grows in step with the air, how long should the flame last under the pickle jar?
maths.explain: The pickle jar holds 4 times as much air. So the flame should last about 4 times as long. 4 times 7 is 28. Real results will be close to this, not exactly on it.
maths.context: This problem uses the jar test, where a candle burned under jars of different sizes.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying lets you predict a result before you test it, and then check whether the pattern holds.

maths.problem: Deepa's results were: small glass 7 seconds, big glass 13 seconds, pickle jar 30 seconds. Her friend says the big glass should have given about 14 seconds, because it held 2 tumblers. Was Deepa's result close enough? Explain.
maths.answer: Yes. 13 is only 1 second away from 14.
maths.explain: 2 times 7 is 14. Deepa got 13. A difference of 1 second is small, and could come from starting the timer a moment late. So the pattern holds: twice the air, about twice the time.
maths.context: This problem compares real results from the jar test with a prediction.
maths.why_maths: Deciding whether a result is close enough to a prediction is how scientists tell a real pattern from small mistakes.

maths.problem: The Moon is about 30 Earths away. On your lime-sized Earth, 5 cm wide, how far away should the grape Moon go?
maths.explain: 30 lots of 5 cm. 30 times 5 is 150. So the grape goes 150 cm, about one and a half metres, from the lime.
maths.context: This problem uses the lime-sized Earth model.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying turns a real distance into a model you can lay out on the floor.

maths.problem: A message from Earth takes 12 minutes to reach a rover on Mars. The team sends 'Stop!' Then they wait to see a picture from the rover showing that it stopped. How long after sending do they see that picture?
maths.explain: The order takes 12 minutes to get there. The picture takes another 12 minutes to come back. 12 plus 12 is 24 minutes.
maths.context: This problem is about the delay in talking to a rover on Mars.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the time out and the time back shows why a far rover cannot be steered moment by moment.

maths.problem: India's first satellite, Aryabhata, was launched in 1975. Chandrayaan-3 landed on the Moon in 2023. How many years apart were they? The first rocket from Thumba was in 1963. How many years before Aryabhata was that?
maths.explain: 2023 take away 1975: from 1975 to 2000 is 25 years, and from 2000 to 2023 is 23 more. 25 plus 23 is 48. Then 1975 take away 1963 is 12.
maths.context: This problem uses India's space timeline.
maths.why_maths: Finding the gaps between years shows how fast India's space programme grew.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, project and challenge was walked through as if done in a city flat. Choices made: the jar test uses a tealight, which sits steady and fits under a small glass; the containers are measured with water first and then dried, because a wet rim can put the flame out. The water-rising version of the candle test was left out on purpose, because it is often explained wrongly. Times are given as rough ranges, and the step says the order matters more than the numbers. The half-lens test needs one bright window and a darkened room; reading glasses for long sight can replace the magnifying glass, and the step warns never to point a lens at the Sun. The ice test needs direct sunlight for half an hour, so it is outside the spine and says to try another day if it is cloudy. Spotting the space station depends on the sky, so it is outside the spine too. The spine is the opening question, the lime-sized Earth, the jar test, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes.

roots.context: We have timed a candle under jars, found how thin the air is, and followed rockets and astronauts beyond it. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Under the bigger jar, your candle burned longer, because it had more air to use. A flame goes out when the oxygen around it runs low. Space has no air, so rockets carry their own oxygen and astronauts carry their own air. Leaving the Earth means taking some of the Earth's air along.
deep_truth.habit: We picture space as more sky, the same air going up and up. But the air is a thin layer close to the ground, with almost nothing above it. We also think of going into space as leaving the Earth behind. No one has gone without bringing the Earth's air, or water to make it.
deep_truth.evidence: In The Jar and the Flame, the tealight went out in a few seconds under a small glass, and lasted several times longer under a big jar. In How Far Is Space?, the edge of space was less than half a millimetre above a lime-sized Earth.

three.who_am_i: You are a body that needs fresh air every few seconds, like the candle needed it under the jar.
three.what_is_life: Plants and algae put oxygen into the air, and you and the candle use it up. Every breath you take was made by living things.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth is wrapped in a thin skin of air, thinner on a lime than four sheets of paper, and beyond it space is almost empty.

roots.thread: All the oxygen in the Earth's air was put there by living things, mostly tiny sea microbes, algae and plants, over a very long time. You breathe it, a candle burns it, and a rocket carries it into space as liquid oxygen. An astronaut's breath on the space station comes from water that was carried up from Earth. So one thin layer of air, made by countless living beings, is shared by every flame and every breath, even the ones beyond the sky.

teachings.teaching: The senses argued about which of them mattered most. Speech left the body for a year, then sight, then hearing, then the mind. Each time, the body lived on. Then breath began to leave, and all the others were pulled out with it, like pegs pulled up by a horse. So they agreed that breath was the greatest.
teachings.link: An astronaut can go without many comforts for a while. But without air for a few minutes, nothing else matters. That is why every spacecraft and spacesuit is built first of all to hold air.

teachings.teaching: In 1990, the Voyager 1 spacecraft looked back from about 6 billion kilometres away and photographed the Earth as a tiny bright dot. Sagan wrote about that dot: 'That's here. That's home. That's us.' Everyone who has ever lived, lived there.
teachings.link: From far enough away, the whole Earth and its thin air are one small dot. Every astronaut carries a little of that dot's air with them, because it is the only air we have.

science.text: Almost all the oxygen in the air was made by living things, mostly algae, bacteria and plants, using sunlight.
Moon rock is nearly half oxygen by weight, locked in minerals. Scientists are testing ways to free it, so future astronauts might not need to carry all their air from Earth.

other_view.view: Air in space is an engineering problem, and engineering can solve it. One day oxygen may be made from Moon rock or from ice on Mars, so people would no longer depend on air from Earth. Calling it a piece of the Earth is a nice thought, but oxygen is oxygen, wherever it comes from.

practice.title: Where does this breath come from?
practice.say: Sit near an open window. Put one hand on your tummy. Breathe in slowly through your nose, and feel the cool air come in. Breathe out slowly, and feel the warm air go out. Do it three more times. Now think: this air came in through the window. Plants and tiny sea algae made its oxygen. An astronaut has to bring every breath from here. Take one more slow breath, and open your eyes.

how_we_found_out.story: Between 1969 and 1972, astronauts brought back about 380 kilograms of rock and dust from the Moon. Scientists tested it for water and found almost none. The few traces they did find, they blamed on damp air from Earth getting into the boxes. So for nearly 40 years, most scientists believed the Moon was bone dry. On 22 October 2008, India launched its first Moon mission, Chandrayaan-1, from Sriharikota. It carried an instrument from NASA called the Moon Mineralogy Mapper, led by the American scientist Carle Pieters. It measured the sunlight bouncing off the Moon. Water soaks up some kinds of light, which our eyes cannot see, and leaves a gap in the reflected light. The Mapper found that gap over large parts of the Moon, strongest near the poles. In September 2009, Pieters and her team reported thin traces of water in the Moon's dust. Two other spacecraft had seen the same. In 2008, scientists also found tiny amounts of water inside glass beads in the old Apollo rocks. In 2018, a study of Chandrayaan-1's data found ice in dark craters at both poles. The dry Moon idea was wrong.
how_we_found_out.who: ISRO's Chandrayaan-1 team, and Carle Pieters, an American scientist who led NASA's Moon Mineralogy Mapper on board
how_we_found_out.when: 1969 to 1972 (Moon rocks brought back), 2008 (Chandrayaan-1 launched), 2009 (water traces reported) and 2018 (polar ice found in its data)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Most scientists thought the Moon was completely dry, because the Apollo rocks seemed to have no water. Chandrayaan-1 measured the light reflected by the Moon and found the gap that water leaves, over much of the surface. Later its data showed ice in the dark polar craters.
